[React Native Automation: Setup Guide](https://maestro.dev/insights/react-native-automation-setup-guide)\n\n# Maestro Mobile Testing Setup for React Native E2E (2024-2025)\n\n## What is Maestro?\n\nMaestro is an open-source mobile UI automation framework designed for end-to-end testing of React Native apps on both iOS and Android.[1] It uses declarative YAML-based syntax to define test flows, eliminating the need for complex imperative code.[1]\n\n## Key Setup Advantages\n\n**Zero Project Dependencies**: Unlike Detox, Maestro requires no npm packages, native modules, or build configuration changes to your React Native project.[1][2] It's a standalone CLI tool that interacts with your app through the device itself.\n\n**No Code Instrumentation**: Tests work with your final bundled binary without modifying JavaScript/TypeScript source code.[3]\n\n**Cross-Platform**: Write once, run on both iOS and Android with the same YAML files.[2]\n\n## Installation \u0026 Requirements\n\nBasic prerequisites include Node.js, npm/yarn, React Native CLI, Android Studio (for Android), and Xcode (for iOS). Java 17+ is also recommended.[5]\n\nInstallation is simple: install the Maestro CLI and you're ready to test.[2]\n\n## Writing Tests\n\nTests are written in human-readable YAML:[1][2]\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;yaml\n- launchApp\n- tapOn: \"Login\"\n- inputText: \"user@example.com\"\n- tapOn: \"Submit\"\n- assertVisible: \"Welcome\"\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nYou can target elements by visible text or &#96;testID&#96; property.[3] For Expo Go development, use &#96;openLink&#96; instead of &#96;launchApp&#96;.[3]\n\n## Key Features\n\n- **Reusable flows**: Break tests into composable, reusable components[2]\n- **Built-in tolerance**: Automatic waiting, retry logic, and element synchronization reduce flakiness[1]\n- **Maestro Studio**: Visual IDE for building tests interactively[1]\n- **Maestro Cloud**: Managed service for running tests at scale on real devices[1]",

{
  "markdown": "# React Native\n\nMaestro provides full support for React Native applications on both Android and iOS. By operating at the accessibility layer, Maestro enables cross-platform testing with a single test suite, requiring zero instrumentation or modifications to your JavaScript/TypeScript source code.\n\n### Technical advantages\n\n- Expo and EAS Ready: Full compatibility with Expo Go, development builds, and EAS Workflows for CI/CD integration.\n- Fast Feedback Loops: Maestro interacts directly with the native views rendered by React Native, providing faster execution than traditional bridge-based testing tools.\n- Zero Library Dependencies: You don't need to install any npm packages (like Detox or Appium drivers) inside your app. Maestro tests the final bundled binary.\n\n### Element interaction strategies\n\nIn React Native, you can target components using visible text or unique identifiers.\n\n#### Interacting by Text\n\nMaestro can interact with any component that displays text content, such as &#96;Button&#96; titles or &#96;Text&#96; components.\n\nIf you have a &#96;Go&#96; button, for example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;javascript\n\u003cButton\n  title=\"Go\"\n  onPress={() =\u003e Alert.alert('Success!')}\n/\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nYou can create a test instruction using that element text:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;yaml\n- tapOn: \"Go\"\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n#### Interacting by testID\n\nUsing visible text is easy but brittle, tests break if you change the label or translate the app. The best practice is to use the &#96;testID&#96; property, which Maestro maps to a unique &#96;id&#96;.\n\nIf you assign a &#96;testID&#96; to any component (Button, View, TextInput, etc.), such as in the example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;javascript\n\u003cTextInput\n  placeholder=\"Username\"\n  testID=\"username_input\"\n/\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWhen creating the test, you can target the identifier directly. This remains stable even if the placeholder or language changes.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;yaml\n- tapOn:\n    id: \"username_input\"\n- inputText: \"maestro_user\"\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### Platform-specific tips\n\n#### Expo Go vs. Standalone Builds\n\nWhen testing with Expo Go, you cannot use &#96;launchApp&#96; with a custom &#96;appId&#96; because your app runs inside the Expo container. Instead, use the &#96;openLink&#96; command with your development URL.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;yaml\n# For Expo Go development\n- openLink: exp://127.0.0.1:19000\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nFor EAS builds or standalone apps, use the standard &#96;launchApp&#96; with your Bundle ID or Package Name.\n\n#### Handling nested components (iOS)\n\nOn iOS, React Native sometimes \"swallows\" touch events if components are deeply nested. If you can't tap an inner element, you can resolve these issues by enabling accessibility for the inner component and disabling it for the outer container.\n\nConsider the following example where you need to tap on the nested text component. The &#96;accessible&#96; for the outer element was disabled and enabled for the inner element.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;javascript\n\u003cTouchableOpacity \n  style={{ borderWidth: 1, margin: 5, padding: 10, backgroundColor: '#ddd' }} \n   accessible={false}\u003e\n  \u003cText\u003eThis is the wrapper button \u003c/Text\u003e\n  \u003cTouchableOpacity \n    style={{ backgroundColor: 'red', padding: 5, width: '50%', marginTop: 10 }} \n     accessible={true}\u003e\n    \u003cText\u003eI'm a small button\u003c/Text\u003e\n  \u003c/TouchableOpacity\u003e\n\u003c/TouchableOpacity\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis way, you can target the inner element using the following command to tap on the Text component.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;yaml\n- tapOn: \"I'm a small button\"\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### Next Steps\n\nIf you don't know how to create tests with Maestro, access the [Quickstart](https://docs.maestro.dev/get-started/quickstart) guide to get up and running in minutes.\n\nTo learn how to create tests, refer to the [Flows](https://app.gitbook.com/s/mS3lsb9jRwfRHqddeRXG/) documentation. If you want to explore Maestro solutions, consult the appropriate documentation:\n\n- [Maestro Cloud](https://app.gitbook.com/s/ky7LkNoLfvcORtXOzzBs/readme)\n- [Maestro CLI](https://app.gitbook.com/s/kq23kwiAeAnHkGJYMGDk/)\n- [Maestro Studio](https://app.gitbook.com/s/eQi66gxHTt2vx4HjhM9V/)",

Summary of what’s in place:

---

**1. Handover read & gaps**

- **Health layer**: Integrations registry, Health Connect service, sync coordinator, sleep pipeline, IntegrationsScreen — all as in the handover.
- **Planned work**: Android = Health Connect only; hide other providers; expand permissions; single upstream for sync.
- **Gap**: The handover doesn’t point to the exact place that builds `sessionsByProvider` for sync. That logic will be wherever `syncHealthData` (or equivalent) calls Google Fit / Samsung; that’s where to restrict Android to Health Connect only.

**2. Maestro setup (no app logic changed)**

- **Doc**: `app/Documentation/MAESTRO_AUTO_TEST_SETUP.md` describes how to give the auto tester everything it needs:
  - **Maestro CLI** — install (Windows/macOS/Linux).
  - **App binary** — build with EAS or `expo run:android` (and later iOS).
  - **App env** — use a **test Supabase project** (and optional **test user**) so runs are repeatable and don’t touch production.
  - **Device/emulator** — Android emulator or device (and later iOS simulator).
  - **Flows** — existing `.maestro/smoke.yaml` and `.maestro/alpha-smoke.yaml`; doc suggests future flows for auth, onboarding, and the rest of the app (settings, analytics, notifications, about, privacy) so one run can cover “every aspect.”

- **Scripts** in `app/package.json`:
  - `npm run e2e` — run all flows in `.maestro/`
  - `npm run e2e:smoke` — smoke only
  - `npm run e2e:alpha` — alpha deep-link tour only  

(Maestro must be installed and a device/emulator available.)

**3. What “everything” means for the tester**

- **Today**: Install Maestro → create test Supabase (and optionally a test user, sign in once on the device) → build app with that env → install APK → run `npm run e2e` from `app/`. Current flows already hit home, sleep, mood, meds, training, mindfulness, meditation, integrations via deep links; they assume the app is already past auth/onboarding.
- **Next**: Add flows (and later `testID`s) for auth, onboarding, settings, analytics, notifications, about, data privacy, and meditation/mindfulness deep-link params so the same runner can repeatedly exercise the full app. The setup doc outlines this and how to plug into CI (e.g. GitHub Actions with secrets for Supabase and test user).

No app code was changed except adding the three npm scripts; the rest is documentation and a clear path to full Maestro coverage.

Download the latest [maestro.zip](https://github.com/mobile-dev-inc/maestro/releases/latest/download/maestro.zip).\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;powershell\nsetx PATH \"%PATH%;C:\\maestro\\bin\"\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n1. The WSL setup requires advanced port configuration, which can introduce issues when testing your app.\n{% endhint %}\n\n{% hint style=\"success\" %}\nIf you encounter problems running your tests using Maestro CLI on WSL, check the troubleshooting guide.\n{% endhint %}\n\n#### 1. Install Java and Maestro\n\nFirst, ensure you have Java 17+ installed.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\nsudo apt update\nsudo apt install openjdk-17-jdk\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nUpdate your environment variables to ensure &#96;JAVA_HOME&#96; is set and Maestro is in your &#96;PATH&#96;. Add the following to your &#96;~/.bashrc&#96; (or &#96;~/.zshrc&#96;):\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\nexport JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-17-openjdk-amd64\nexport PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH\nexport PATH=$PATH:$HOME/.maestro/bin\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nReload your configuration:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\nsource ~/.bashrc\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nNow, install Maestro:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\ncurl -fsSL \"https://get.maestro.mobile.dev\" | bash\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n#### 2. Setup Android environment\n\nSince you cannot run the Android Studio GUI directly in WSL easily, you need to set up the Android command-line tools manually. This enables you to access and control the Android emulator running on Windows.\n\n1. Create the Android directory:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\nmkdir -p $HOME/Android/cmdline-tools\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n1. Download the latest [command line tools for Linux](https://developer.android.com/studio#command-tools) (zip/targz) and unzip it. Configure the environment by adding the following to your &#96;~/.bashrc&#96;:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\n# --- Android PATH ---\nexport ANDROID_HOME=$HOME/Android\nexport PATH=$PATH:$ANDROID_HOME/cmdline-tools/latest/bin\nexport PATH=$PATH:$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n1. Reload the terminal running:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\nsource ~/.bashrc.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n1. Install the platform tools:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\nsdkmanager --install \"platform-tools\"\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n#### 3. Connect to Windows Emulator\n\nAndroid Emulators run on the Windows host. You need to bridge ADB from WSL to Windows.\n\nOn Windows (PowerShell):\n\nStart the ADB server to allow external connections. \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;powershell\nadb -a -P 5037 nodaemon server\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIf successful, the command will not show any output and will just sit there. This is normal! Do not close this PowerShell window, as it keeps the connection alive.\n\nAfter starting the server and proceeding to WSL, you must have an active Android device. Open Android Studio on Windows.\n\n{% hint style=\"info\" %}\n\n#### &#96;adb&#96; is not recognized?\n\nIf you see an error saying &#96;The term 'adb' is not recognized&#96;, it means the Android SDK platform-tools are not in your Windows PATH.\n\nAdd to PATH via PowerShell (Recommended)\n\nRun this command in PowerShell to permanently add the path for your user:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;powershell\n[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable(\"Path\", $env:Path + \";$env:LOCALAPPDATA\\Android\\Sdk\\platform-tools\", \"User\")\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nRestart your PowerShell terminal after running this command.\n\nManual method\n\n1. Click New and paste: &#96;%LOCALAPPDATA%\\Android\\Sdk\\platform-tools&#96;.\n{% endhint %}\n2. Edit the &#96;Path&#96; variable.\n3. Try to start the ADB server again.\n{% endhint %}\n\nOn WSL:\n\nConfigure ADB to connect to the Windows host IP. **New file: `app/Documentation/MAESTRO_QUICKSTART.md`** — full step-by-step runbook.

**Summary of steps:**

1. **Prerequisites (one-time)**  
   Java 17+, Android SDK with `adb` in PATH, and a device or emulator. Optional: add `platform-tools` to PATH if `adb` isn’t found.

2. **Install Maestro CLI**  
   - **Option A:** If you have Git Bash/WSL: `curl -fsSL "https://get.maestro.mobile.dev" | bash`, then add the install dir to PATH.  
   - **Option B (PowerShell):** Download `maestro.zip` from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/mobile-dev-inc/maestro/releases/latest), extract to e.g. `C:\maestro`, then:
   ```powershell
   setx PATH "%PATH%;C:\maestro\bin"
   ```
   Restart PowerShell and run `maestro --version`.

3. **Put Reclaim on the device**  
   Either `cd c:\Reclaim\app` and `npx expo run:android`, or build with EAS preview, download the APK, and `adb install path\to\build.apk`.

4. **App state**  
   On that same device, open Reclaim, sign in to alpha Supabase, and finish onboarding so the app is on the main (tabs) UI.

5. **Check device**  
   Run `adb devices` and fix any “unauthorized” by accepting USB debugging on the device.

6. **Run Maestro**  
   From `c:\Reclaim\app`:
   ```powershell
   maestro test .maestro/smoke.yaml
   maestro test .maestro/alpha-smoke.yaml
   ```
   Or run everything with:
   ```powershell
   npm run e2e
   ```

The quickstart doc also has a short troubleshooting table and “Confirm it worked” notes. The main setup doc now starts with a link to **MAESTRO_QUICKSTART.md** for the runbook.

Summary of what changed:

**1. No more white screens**  
- Both flows now use **`extendedWaitUntil`** and wait for the **“Open navigation menu”** header (up to 30 seconds) before any screenshot.  
- So screenshots only run after the app has finished loading/rebundling and the main UI is visible.

**2. Real navigation by tapping**  
- **alpha-smoke** no longer uses deep links. It:
  - Opens the **drawer** (tap “Open navigation menu”).
  - Taps each item in turn: **Sleep**, **Mood**, **Meds**, **Exercise**, **Mindfulness**, **Meditation**, **Integrations**, **Settings**, **Notifications**, **About**.
  - Takes a screenshot on each screen (01-home through 11-about).
- So the test actually **clicks through** the app like a user.

**3. Logging**  
- Maestro logs **every step** in the terminal (launch, wait, tap, screenshot, etc.). When you run `maestro test .maestro/alpha-smoke.yaml` you’ll see each action as it runs.

**4. smoke.yaml**  
- **smoke** still does a minimal check: launch → wait for “Open navigation menu” (30s) → one screenshot. So the quick smoke test also avoids white-screen captures.

**Files updated**  
- `app/.maestro/smoke.yaml` — wait for app ready, then one screenshot.  
- `app/.maestro/alpha-smoke.yaml` — wait for app ready, then tap through the drawer and screenshot each screen.  
- `app/Documentation/MAESTRO_QUICKSTART.md` — updated to describe the new behavior.

Run again with:

```powershell
cd c:\Reclaim\app
maestro test .maestro/alpha-smoke.yaml
```

You should see the device open the drawer, jump to each screen, and get real screenshots of each. If “Open navigation menu” isn’t found within 30s (e.g. very slow rebundle), increase the `timeout` in the flow or ensure the app is already loaded before starting the test.
